/*
# SimpleLayout — stack children along an axis

The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along
`axis`, in child order, `spacing` apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis
and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row
with the ordinary `y = center`. Invisible children are skipped and their
space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the slot it would occupy, so
re-showing it needs no special case. A `Spacer` child flexes to absorb the
run's slack along the axis (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on
each side centers the run).

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one
pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ]
    ]
```

## axis
Which way children stack: `y` (the default) or `x`. **A bare literal, not a string** —
`axis = x`, and note that `x` here is the axis token, not the position attribute.

## spacing
The gap between adjacent children. **Negative overlaps them**, which is how a stack of
cards or avatars is built.

## place()
The whole strategy: one box per laid child, positioned along the axis in child order.
**The cross axis and every size stay the children's own** — a child centres itself
across a row with the ordinary `y = center`. Override it in a subclass for custom
geometry; a `Layout`'s `place()` **may** aggregate over children, which is the one place
that is allowed.
*/

class SimpleLayout extends Layout [
    axis: Axis = y,
    spacing: number = 0,

    place() {
        const axis = this.axis
        const size = axis == "x" ? "width" : "height"
        const kids = this.laid()
        const flexing = (c) => (c).flexes === true

        // slack, only when someone flexes: the view's extent along the axis
        // minus the rigid content and the gaps between visible children
        let each = 0
        let flexN = 0
        for (const c of kids) if (c.visible && flexing(c)) flexN = flexN + 1
        if (flexN > 0) {
            let content = 0
            let visN = 0
            for (const c of kids) {
                if (!c.visible) continue
                visN = visN + 1
                if (!flexing(c)) content = content + (c)[size]
            }
            const extent = this.view == null ? 0 : (this.view)[size]
            each = Math.max(0, (extent - content - this.spacing * Math.max(0, visN - 1)) / flexN)
        }

        let pos = 0
        return kids.map((c) => {
            const flex = c.visible && flexing(c)
            const box = (axis == "x" ? ({ x: pos }) : ({ y: pos }))
            if (flex) box[axis == "x" ? "w" : "h"] = each
            if (c.visible) pos = pos + (flex ? each : (c)[size]) + this.spacing
            return box
            })
        }
    ]

/*
# Icon — the drawn mark

A small monochrome mark, **drawn** rather than typed. Fonts are not UI objects:
their glyphs are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on
every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a `✓` sits on the
text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The house
already knew this in three places before it had a name for it (`Checkbox.mark`,
`Menu.check`, `Combobox.disc` are all drawn); this is that decision, stated once.

### Writing one

Subclass and override `draw`. Author the shape in a **16×16 box** — `unit`
converts it to whatever size the host asked for:

```declare-fragment
class SparkIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(unit, unit)
        d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit
        d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke()
        }
    ]
```

Overriding a **method** is the refinement path that works — re-opening an
inherited child is not (`cap:` on a `Button` subclass fails at instantiate), so
the shape lives in `draw` and everything adjustable is a slot.

### Size changes the drawing, not the shape

Every icon is ONE path. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing
redrawn at a breakpoint: `unit` scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for,
so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly.

The **stroke** is the deliberate exception. `d.lineWidth = weight / unit` sits
*inside* `d.scale(unit, unit)`, so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant
`weight` in **device pixels at every size**. An icon's line therefore matches the
1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows.

The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5%
at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px, which is every site in this corpus, that is
invisible. Past ~32 an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a
mark — so **this set is built for chrome sizes**, and a large display icon (an
empty-state mark, an about-box graphic) would want the opposite: `d.lineWidth =
weight` *outside* the scale, so the line grows with the drawing. Real icon
systems take a third road and redraw per optical size range; that is a bigger
undertaking than this set needs.

`test/probe/iconbook.declare` shows the ramp — the same chevron and bulb at 16,
24, 32, 48 and 64 — if the tradeoff ever needs re-judging.

### What is NOT an Icon

Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before
reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification
swell, they are polychrome (`gradient(hue1, hue2)` behind a hue-parameterised
drawing), and their **width animates every frame**. Each of those alone rules
them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and
reads spindly; `ink` is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing
this set forbids.

The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is
**chrome vocabulary versus identity**. A mark that says *close*, *expand*,
*checked*, *this is the dark theme* belongs here, at a size the host states.
A mark that says *this is Calendar* does not, and belongs to the app that owns
the identity.

Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows
take `WindowIcon` and `CodeIcon` from this set, while its dock keeps `DockIcon`.

### Two rules

**Scale inside the body, never with the View's `scale`.** A recording rasterizes
into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution
(`dom-backend.ts` `rasterize()`), while `scale` is a CSS transform applied
*after* — so `scale = { width / 16 }` would rasterize 16 pixels and stretch them.
Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is most of them. Scaling
inside the recording allocates the raster at true size instead.

**Never animate an icon's `width`.** Reading size inside `draw` makes the
recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records AND reallocates the backing
canvas every frame, which is what dragged the dock's magnification from 60 to
~25fps (`adaptive-draw-cache.md`). A static size re-records once and costs
nothing after. Measured: 120 icons re-recording their *content* every frame runs
frame-bound at 16.6ms, cheaper than the 120 text glyphs they replace.

Colour is not a rule — `ink` follows the prevailing text colour, so an icon beside
a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a
menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

## ink
The mark's colour. Follows the **prevailing `textColor`**, so an icon beside a muted
label goes muted on its own. **The trap: that slot falls back to black platform-wide**,
so an icon in a context that never states a text colour renders black and vanishes on a
dark surface. State `ink` unless you know the context sets one — `IconHost` does it for
every icon built by name.

## weight
Stroke width in **final device pixels, not authored ones**. Divide by `unit` inside
`draw` (`d.lineWidth = weight / unit`) and the scale cancels, so the line lands at a
constant weight at every size and matches the 1px rules and text it sits among.

## unit
The 16-box-to-host-size scale factor. **Multiply the path by it; divide the stroke by
it.** Every icon is one path at one size, scaled — there are no per-size variants.

## isIcon
**Internal.** The marker a layout keys on to place an icon without knowing which shape
it is — not API.
*/

/*
# IconHost — a named icon, materialized

   A control names its icon (`iconLeft = TrashIcon`) rather than nesting one,
   because a control is a leaf and everything else about it is an attribute — and
   because an attribute is the one form where AUTHORED and BOUND are the same
   mechanism. `IconHost` is what turns that name into a live view, through the
   same `app.createView` seam the menu's `iconKind` already uses.

   It reserves no space when empty, so a control's `contentWidth` measures only
   the slots that are actually filled and an icon-less button needs no special
   case.

   LIMITATION, deliberate for now: the name is consumed once, at construction.
   A control whose icon must CHANGE at runtime (a play/pause toggle) is not
   served by this yet — that needs a name-valued slot the runtime re-materializes
   on change, which is a runtime feature, not a library one. Every site in this
   corpus names its icon statically.

## kind
The icon **class name** to build (`"TrashIcon"`). `""` builds nothing and the host
collapses to zero width, so an icon-less control needs no special case. **Consumed once,
at construction** — assigning a new name later does not re-materialize the icon. A name
that is only ever computed needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build.

## ink
The colour handed to the icon this host builds. **`createView` cannot pass attributes,
so a prevailing slot is the only channel that reaches it** — this publishes `textColor`
for exactly that. Defaults to `theme.text` rather than the platform's inherited black,
which is what stops a host-built icon from rendering invisibly on a dark surface.

## onInit
Builds the named icon. Fires once.
*/

class IconHost extends View [
    kind: string = "",
    width  = { classroot.kind == "" ? 0 : this.iconSize },
    height = { this.iconSize },
    y = center,
    visible = { classroot.kind != "" },

    // THE INK CHANNEL. `createView` cannot pass attributes, so the only way to
    // reach the icon it builds is a PREVAILING slot — and the one `Icon.ink`
    // reads is `textColor`. Publishing it here is what lets a host state its
    // ink at all.
    //
    // The default matters more than it looks: prevailing `textColor` falls back
    // to 0x000000 platform-wide, so an icon that inherited it rendered BLACK —
    // fine on a light surface by luck, invisible on a dark one. Every
    // host-created icon in the corpus was doing that. `theme.text` is a floor
    // that is never invisible in either palette.

    ink: Color = { this.theme.text },
    textColor = { classroot.ink },

    onInit() { if (this.kind != "") this.root.createView(this.kind, this, ({ })) }
    ]


class Icon extends View [
    // The marker a layout keys on, so a control can place its icon without
    // caring which shape it is (the Segment/Segmented discipline).

    isIcon: boolean = true,

    // Size comes from the CONTEXT: `iconSize` is prevailing, so a menu states 16
    // once and every icon in every row answers. A use site may override it.

    width  = { this.iconSize },
    height = { this.width },
    y = center,

    // Follows the PREVAILING text colour, so an icon beside a muted label goes
    // muted on its own. The trap: that slot falls back to 0x000000 platform-wide,
    // so an icon in a context which never states a text colour renders BLACK and
    // disappears on a dark surface. State `ink` unless you know the context sets
    // one — `IconHost` does it for every icon built by name.

    ink: Color = { this.textColor },
    weight: number = 1.6,        // stroke width in FINAL pixels, not authored ones

    // 16-box → host size. Multiply the path by this; divide the stroke by it, so
    // the line keeps its true weight instead of scaling with the drawing.

    unit: number = { this.width / 16 }
    ]

/*
# Core icons

The marks the chrome uses everywhere: a chevron, a check, a close, plus/minus,
and the menu's help bulb. Each is authored in a 16×16 box and scaled to the
host's `iconSize` inside its recording (see `icon.declare`).

Geometry is a property of the SET, not of the site: one stroke weight, round caps
and joins throughout, one path per shape. Before this, the corpus drew a
checkmark two ways (stroke 2.5 mitered in `Checkbox`, 1.8 round in `Menu`) and a
chevron at least six, three of them inside the library. Ink stays local — a menu
row inverts its check on the hot row, a checkbox always uses `accentText`.
*/



/*
# ChevronIcon

The **disclosure** mark: a menu drops, a pane opens, a select expands. Every
disclosure in the chrome is this one class turned by its `dir`, which is what makes
them agree. For a direction that is itself the state — a sort order, a trend — reach
for `ArrowIcon` instead; the two must not look alike.

## dir
The resting orientation: `"down"` (the default), `"up"`, `"left"` or `"right"`. Sugar
over `angle`.

## angle
The rotation in radians, and **the primitive, so it can be sprung** — an `Accordion`
twisty turns in step with its pane sliding open rather than snapping between two
states. The turn lives in the recording deliberately: the mark rotates inside its
16-box while the box stays put. (The View-level `rotation` attribute turns the whole
box — the wrong tool for a glyph whose frame should not move.)

## draw()
Renders the chevron. Override to replace the mark while keeping the class's role.
*/

class ChevronIcon extends Icon [
    dir: string = "down",                       // down | up | left | right
    angle: number = { classroot.dir == "up" ? Math.PI
                    : classroot.dir == "left" ? Math.PI / 2
                    : classroot.dir == "right" ? -Math.PI / 2 : 0 },

    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.lineJoin = "round"
        d.save()
        d.translate(8, 8)
        d.rotate(this.angle)
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(-3.5, -1.75)
        d.lineTo(0, 1.75)
        d.lineTo(3.5, -1.75)
        d.stroke()
        d.restore()
        }
    ]


/*
# ArrowIcon

An arrow, **not a chevron** — the two mean different things and must not look alike.
A chevron *discloses*; an arrow points at a direction that **is itself the state**:
sort ascending, a trend, a transfer. The shaft is what a chevron lacks. Tracker had
the two adjacent — a sort-direction control beside a sort-menu popper — and one shape
for both read as a mistake.

## dir
Which way it points: `"up"` (the default), `"down"`, `"left"` or `"right"`.

## angle
The rotation in radians, sprungable like `ChevronIcon`'s.

## draw()
Renders the arrow.
*/

class ArrowIcon extends Icon [
    dir: string = "up",                         // up | down | left | right
    angle: number = { classroot.dir == "down" ? Math.PI
                    : classroot.dir == "left" ? -Math.PI / 2
                    : classroot.dir == "right" ? Math.PI / 2 : 0 },

    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.lineJoin = "round"
        d.save()
        d.translate(8, 8)
        d.rotate(this.angle)
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(0, 5.2); d.lineTo(0, -5.2)     // the shaft is what a chevron lacks
        d.moveTo(-3.6, -1.6); d.lineTo(0, -5.2); d.lineTo(3.6, -1.6)
        d.stroke()
        d.restore()
        }
    ]


/*
# CheckIcon

The tick — a checked menu row, a `Checkbox`'s mark, a confirmation. **Ink stays
local**: a menu row inverts its check on the highlighted row while a checkbox always
uses the accent text colour, so the host sets `ink` rather than the icon assuming it.

## draw()
Renders the tick. Before this class the corpus drew a checkmark two ways — stroke 2.5
mitered in `Checkbox`, 1.8 round in `Menu` — which is the drift one shape ends.
*/

class CheckIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.lineJoin = "round"
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(3, 8.5)
        d.lineTo(6.5, 12)
        d.lineTo(13, 4.5)
        d.stroke()
        }
    ]


/*
# CloseIcon

The dismiss mark: a window close box, a chip's remove affordance, a dialog's corner.

## draw()
Renders the cross.
*/

class CloseIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(4.5, 4.5); d.lineTo(11.5, 11.5)
        d.moveTo(11.5, 4.5); d.lineTo(4.5, 11.5)
        d.stroke()
        }
    ]


/*
# PlusIcon

Add. Pairs with `MinusIcon` at the same stroke and cap, so a stepper's two ends match.

## draw()
Renders the plus.
*/

class PlusIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(8, 3.5); d.lineTo(8, 12.5)
        d.moveTo(3.5, 8); d.lineTo(12.5, 8)
        d.stroke()
        }
    ]


/*
# MinusIcon

Remove, and the partially-checked state of a tri-state box. Pairs with `PlusIcon`.

## draw()
Renders the bar.
*/

class MinusIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.strokeStyle = this.ink
        d.lineWidth = this.weight / this.unit
        d.lineCap = "round"
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(3.5, 8); d.lineTo(12.5, 8)
        d.stroke()
        }
    ]


/*
# LightbulbIcon

The macOS Help affordance — **Apple's own `lightbulb`, ported exactly** rather than
redrawn: the outline was lifted from the live symbol at 1024pt and normalised to the
16-box.

## draw()
Renders the bulb. **This one mark is filled, and does not answer to `weight`** — an SF
Symbol is a filled contour with the stroke baked into the outline, so matching Apple
means adopting a shape, not a stroke. There is no stroke here to widen. The set's own
drawn bulb is the alternative; this is the port.
*/

// Ported EXACTLY. Not
// redrawn from a screenshot and not approximated: the outline was lifted from
// the live symbol (`NSSymbolImageRep.outlinePath` at 1024pt, 29 elements,
// bounds 1338 × 2327), normalised so the mark is 16 units tall — 9.20 wide,
// centred at x + 3.40. No y-flip: `outlinePath` already counts DOWN, like this
// canvas — flipping it stood the bulb on its head, which the overlay caught and
// a glance would not have. `test/probe/ref/render.swift` regenerates the
// reference it was measured against.
//
// It is FILLED, and that is not a lapse in a stroked set: an SF Symbol IS a
// filled contour, with the stroke baked into the outline at a chosen weight.
// Matching Apple exactly therefore means adopting a shape, not a stroke — so
// this one mark does not answer to `weight`, and cannot, because there is no
// stroke to widen. The set's own bulb is the alternative; this is the port.
//
// What the port changes, measured against the drawing it replaces: the filament
// is gone (Apple has none), the glass is a continuous teardrop rather than an
// arc with a gap, and the base is three tapering bars at 11.48 / 13.19 / 14.68
// rather than three equal rules.

class LightbulbIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(this.unit, this.unit)
        d.fillStyle = this.ink
        d.beginPath()
        d.moveTo(3.4, 4.235)
        d.bezierCurveTo(3.4, 6.876, 4.982, 7.529, 5.422, 12.115)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.449, 12.363, 5.587, 12.521, 5.848, 12.521)
        d.lineTo(10.152, 12.521)
        d.bezierCurveTo(10.42, 12.521, 10.558, 12.363, 10.585, 12.115)
        d.bezierCurveTo(11.025, 7.529, 12.6, 6.876, 12.6, 4.235)
        d.bezierCurveTo(12.6, 1.863, 10.572, 0.0, 8.0, 0.0)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.428, 0.0, 3.4, 1.863, 3.4, 4.235)
        d.closePath()
        d.moveTo(4.438, 4.235)
        d.bezierCurveTo(4.438, 2.379, 6.068, 1.038, 8.0, 1.038)
        d.bezierCurveTo(9.932, 1.038, 11.562, 2.379, 11.562, 4.235)
        d.bezierCurveTo(11.562, 6.209, 10.255, 6.676, 9.636, 11.483)
        d.lineTo(6.37, 11.483)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.745, 6.676, 4.438, 6.209, 4.438, 4.235)
        d.closePath()
        d.moveTo(5.827, 14.006)
        d.lineTo(10.18, 14.006)
        d.bezierCurveTo(10.407, 14.006, 10.578, 13.827, 10.578, 13.6)
        d.bezierCurveTo(10.578, 13.38, 10.407, 13.202, 10.18, 13.202)
        d.lineTo(5.827, 13.202)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.6, 13.202, 5.422, 13.38, 5.422, 13.6)
        d.bezierCurveTo(5.422, 13.827, 5.6, 14.006, 5.827, 14.006)
        d.closePath()
        d.moveTo(8.0, 16.0)
        d.bezierCurveTo(9.066, 16.0, 9.953, 15.477, 10.021, 14.687)
        d.lineTo(5.985, 14.687)
        d.bezierCurveTo(6.034, 15.477, 6.927, 16.0, 8.0, 16.0)
        d.closePath()
        d.fill()
        }
    ]

/*
# Menu

The record-driven menu (planes.md §4–§6): items are DATA — the component
arranges; the author never composes rows. The standard record covers real OS
menus:

    { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props? }

- `key` renders right-aligned (display only — registration is the Keys
  service's, later).
- `icon: "ClassName"` names an icon class for the leading column, and the label
  shifts right to make room — the same vocabulary `Segmented`'s choices use.

  This was THREE mechanisms before the icon set landed: a text glyph (`"◐"`), a
  hardcoded `"lightbulb"` that special-cased its way to a drawn bulb because no
  glyph matched, and `iconKind` naming a class. The middle one was the tell —
  somebody needed a mark the fonts could not give, and the escape hatch already
  existed. One field now; a COMPUTED name needs its class kept with
  `use [ Name ]`, since no static reference reaches it.
- `enabled: false` dims the row (theme.disabledOpacity) and refuses pick.
- `{ divider: true }` is a separator line.
- `submenu: [ …records… ]` marks a cascade (the ▸ arrow; the cascade itself
  lands with the roving-keyboard stage).
- `kind: "ClassName"` renders the row's CONTENT with a named author class
  (app.createView — keep data-only classes with `use [ Name ]`), passed
  `props` as its datapath context. Behavior stays the row's: highlight,
  pick, keyboard are the menu's, always.

Declared ONCE, opened by many (the worked example): rows carry
`onContextMenu(e) { app.rowMenu.openAt(this, e) }`; the menu's `items`
constraint derives from `opener` — per-row variation with zero per-row
instances, live while open. `openAt` point-positions (the context-menu
rule); `openFor` drops below a control (the attached-menu rule); both
RAISE the menu (promotion — order is a slot) and clamp inside the app.

Dismissal: the BACKDROP (a full-app child under the panel) — a press
outside closes AND is swallowed, the Mac rule (planes.md §12.1, resolved
for v1); Escape closes; pick closes after delivery.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130,
    chose: string = "",
    edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }),
                            ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C", checked: true }),
                            ({ divider: true }),
                            ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

## items
The rows, as **records — never children**. A menu arranges its own rows, so handing it
views is not merely discouraged, there is nowhere to put them. The record is
`{ id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props? }`;
a plain array is fine (no `Dataset` required). Because it is an ordinary attribute it
can be a constraint — **derive it from `opener` and one menu serves every row of a
table**, live while it is open.

## opener
The view this menu was opened for, set by `openAt`/`openFor` and cleared on close.
**The key to declaring one menu and opening it from many places**: read it in the
`items` constraint to vary the rows per opener, with no per-opener instance.

## shown
Whether the menu is up. Read it; **open through `openAt`/`openFor` rather than
assigning it**, or the menu appears unplaced, unraised, and without its keyboard claim.
Closing by assignment skips the cascade teardown for the same reason.

## picked()
**The delivery seam — override it at the use site.** Receives the picked row's `id`,
and the id is the whole message. Called *after* the menu has left the screen, so a slow
action can never freeze an open menu.

## openFor()
Opens the menu **anchored below a control**, flipping above it when there is not room
below and more room above — the native select discipline. The attached-menu rule; what
`Control.menu` uses.

## openAt()
Opens the menu **at the pointer**, given the serving view and the pointer event — the
context-menu rule. Clamped inside the app like any placement. `ContextMenu` wraps this
as `open`.

## close()
Takes the menu down, closes any cascade under it, and releases the keyboard claim.

## pick()
Delivers a row: **dismisses first, then delivers**, one painted frame later — the
native menu contract, and the reason a long-running action cannot leave a menu stranded
on screen. A submenu routes to the root so the whole chain closes as one.

## activeRow
The row the keyboard rover currently highlights, or null when the pointer is driving.
Read-only in practice.

## hasIcons
Whether any row carries an `icon` — which is what decides the icon gutter exists at
all. **A menu with no icons has no gutter**, and the text edge moves accordingly.

## textEdge
The x every row's label starts at — one line for the whole menu, icons or not, and what
a `kind` row must align its own content to.

## expectedHeight()
The panel's height *before it has been laid out*, measured when it exists and estimated
from the record count when it does not. The flip-above decision cannot wait for a
settle, which is why this exists.

## place()
Positions the panel from **root-space** coordinates, converting into the parent's space
and clamping inside the app — so a menu works declared at App level or inside a
component. The chain offset is snapshotted at open: menu chrome does not move while a
menu is up.

## isRoot
False on a cascade child. The root owns the backdrop, the deferred delivery, and the
Escape-closes-everything behaviour; a submenu delegates all three upward.

## rootMenu
The root of this menu's cascade chain — null on the root itself.

## child
The one lazily-created submenu instance, reused across every row that cascades. **A
`Menu` cannot declare a `Menu` child** (it would recurse), so the cascade is built by
name at first use.

## openSub()
Opens a row's `submenu`, creating the shared child menu on first use and placing it
alongside the row.

## closeSub()
Closes the cascade under this menu, if any.

## rootClose()
Closes the entire chain from wherever it is called — what Escape and an outside press
both do.

## step()
Moves the keyboard rover by ±1 over the pickable rows, skipping dividers, disabled rows
and custom-content rows, and scrolls the landing row into view.

## pickActive()
Picks the roved row — Enter's action. On a row with a `submenu` it enters the cascade
instead.

## enterSub()
Enters the roved row's submenu and puts the rover on its first row — ArrowRight's action.

## driveSub()
**Internal.** Pushes items, placement and delivery into the shared child menu.

## closeIt()
**Internal.** Null-safe close, the untyped seam across files.

## subShown()
**Internal.** Whether a cascade child is currently up, so the deeper menu takes the keys.

## rowsOf()
**Internal.** The row views of a panel body, for the rover's walk.

## revealRow()
**Internal.** Scrolls a roved row into view in a menu long enough to scroll.

## pickRow()
**Internal.** Picks or enters a specific row view.

## enterRow()
**Internal.** Enters a specific row's submenu.

## stepIn()
**Internal.** Puts the rover on a freshly opened cascade's first row.

## offX
**Internal.** The parent chain's x offset, snapshotted at open.

## offY
**Internal.** The parent chain's y offset, snapshotted at open.

    items: array = null,
    opener: View = null,
    shown: boolean = false,

    // anything is checked or even checkable; an ICON column exists only when
    // some row in THIS menu carries an icon (no icons → no gutter at all);
    // and the TEXT LEFT EDGE is one line for every row, icons or not.
    // Custom (kind) rows align their content to the same text edge.
    //   check col: x 7..24   ·   icon col (iff hasIcons): x 24..44
    //   text edge: 50 with icons, 24 without

    // The 6px between the icon column and the text edge is measured, not picked
    // (2026-08-03). The Mac leaves about 7.5pt from its icon BOX to its text,
    // but its symbols carry side bearing — only the widest glyph in a menu comes
    // within 8.5pt of the label, while a padlock or a power mark sits 10–11pt
    // clear. Ours are drawn to fill their 16px box, so every row landed at that
    // tight extreme at once, uniformly, which is what read as crowding: the
    // right number to match is the Mac's AVERAGE air (≈9.5pt), not its minimum.

    textEdge: number = { this.hasIcons ? 50 : 24 },

    // cannot declare a Menu child without recursing), reused across rows;
    // rootMenu threads to the chain's root (null ON the root). activeRow is
    // the keyboard rover's highlight. View-typed slots can't see Menu
    // members, so all child-driving goes through ANY-typed method params —
    // the untyped seam, used deliberately.

    isRoot: boolean = true,
    rootMenu: Menu = null,
    child: Menu = null,
    activeRow: View = null,

    // the delivery seam — the app overrides; the id is the whole message

    picked(id: string) { },

    // the panel's height BEFORE first paint: measured when it exists, else
    // estimated from the records (the flip decision can't wait a settle)

    expectedHeight() -> number {
        const est = (this.items ?? []).length * (typeof this.theme.menuRow == "number" ? this.theme.menuRow : 26) + 10

    openAt(v: View, e: PointerEvent) {
        const o = v.rootOrigin()
        this.place(o.x + e.x, o.y + e.y)
        this.opener = v
        this.shown = true
        Keys.navClaim(this, true)
        this.raise()
        },

    // and there's more room above, it emerges ABOVE instead (the native
    // select discipline). place() still clamps whatever remains.

    openFor(v: View) {
        const o = v.rootOrigin()
        const h = this.expectedHeight()
        const below = o.y + v.height + 4
        const up = below + h > this.root.height - 4 && o.y - 4 - h >= 4

        this.opener = v
        this.shown = true
        Keys.navClaim(this, true)
        this.raise()
        },

    // `rootOrigin()` — THE one scroll-aware walk, so a serving view inside a
    // scrolled pane anchors where the user SEES it) and converts to
    // parent-space, so a Menu works declared at App level OR inside a
    // component (MenuBar owns one). The chain offset is snapshotted at
    // open — menu chrome doesn't move while a menu is up.

    offX: number = 0,
    offY: number = 0,

    place(x: number, y: number) {

        const py = po.y
        this.offX = px
        this.offY = py

    close() {

    pickRow(r: object) {

# ContextMenu

The right-click / long-press menu (component-briefs.md §4 — D8 RULED): Menu's
machinery WHOLE — overlay, raise, pointer-anchored placement with viewport
clamping, the Mac light-dismiss rule (outside press closes AND is swallowed),
Escape closes the chain — with a gesture-opened entry. No new overlay
machinery, by the brief's own constraint: if ContextMenu ever needs something
Menu lacks, Menu grows it and both ride.

Declared ONCE, opened by many. The SERVING view declares the gesture — that
declaration is what routes it (the claim model: `contextMenu` engages the
right-click/two-finger path, `hold` is the touch long-press gate, and each
engages only where a handler is declared). The whole wiring is two lines on
the view the menu serves:

    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { … }, picked(id: string) { … } ],
    …
    Row [ …,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) } ]

`open(v, e)` anchors at the pointer (view-relative event coordinates walked to
root space) and clamps inside the app — Menu's own placement discipline. Items
are the standard Menu records — written lists or derived from the opener
(`items = { … opener … }` for per-row menus with zero per-row instances);
picking delivers through `picked(id)` and closes.

Everything else — `items`, `opener`, `picked`, the rover, the cascade, dismissal — is
`Menu`'s, documented there.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "",
    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { [ ({ id: "open", label: "Open" }),
                                      ({ id: "rename", label: "Rename" }),
                                      ({ divider: true }),
                                      ({ id: "delete", label: "Delete" }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 44, cornerRadius = 8, fill = darkslategray,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        Text [ x = 12, y = center, text = "Right-click or hold me" ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.chose == "" ? "—" : app.chose } ]
    ]
```

## open()
Opens the menu **anchored at the pointer**, given the serving view and the pointer
event — `Menu.openAt` under the name the two-line wiring reads best with. **The serving
view declares the gesture, and that declaration is what routes it**: `onContextMenu`
engages the right-click and two-finger path, `onHold` the touch long-press. Neither
engages anywhere a handler is not declared, so a context menu costs nothing on views
that do not offer one.

## isContextMenu
**Internal.** The marker that identifies this as a context menu — not API.
*/

# Control

The interaction-state base every stateful control extends (docs/system-design/components-baseline.md,
Contract 3). It owns how the pointer, keyboard, and focus relate to this view — and
nothing semantic: `checked`, `value`, and their kin live on the concrete control.

The pointer half is the language's now: `hovered` and `pressed` are View's read-only
interaction intrinsics (chain-based, touch-correct, cancel-safe). What Control adds is
the CONTROL policy on top of them, as derivations every concrete control reads:

- `hot` / `down` — the styling pair: the intrinsics gated by `disabled`, with the
  keyboard-activation `flash` folded into `down`. Style against these, not the raw
  intrinsics, and a disabled control never lights up.
- `disabled` — inert: not focusable, no activation; concrete controls gate on it.
- keyboard — Space or Enter on the focused control activates it, the same `press()`
  path a pointer uses, acknowledged by flashing the pressed look.

It also owns the two things every labelled control was improvising:

- `iconLeft` / `iconRight` — decoration, by class name. A concrete control lays
  them out; Control only declares that they exist, so `Button` and `Segment`
  answer to one vocabulary.
- `menu` — the ROLE of dropping a menu. Not decoration: fifteen sites across the
  corpus call `someMenu.openFor(control)`, and the disclosure mark for that one
  role was drawn five different ways or omitted (a glyph inside the label string
  in five places, a private chevron in two, a separate `Text` in one, nothing in
  `MenuBar` and `DataGrid`). Nobody chose those differences. Setting `menu` gets
  the mark, the anchored open, the held-open styling, and Down-to-open together,
  which is the part a hand-rolled copy gets wrong one piece at a time.

Extend it to make your own control a first-class one — focusable, keyboard-activated,
and styled off the same state pair as everything the library ships:

```declare

    n: number = 0,
    fill = { down ? theme.controlPressed : hot ? theme.controlHover : theme.control },
    press() { n = n + 1 },
    onClick() { if (!disabled) press() },
    t: Text [ x = center, y = center, fontSize = 13, text = { "" + classroot.n } ]
    ]


App [ Stepper [ x = 20, y = 20 ] ]
```

## disabled
Inert: not focusable, no activation, and the gate folded into `hot`/`down` so a
disabled control never lights up. **Constrain it rather than assigning it**
(`disabled = { app.muted }`) — it is ordinary derived state. Concrete controls also
dim themselves against `theme.disabledOpacity`.

## hot
Hover under control policy — `hovered` gated by `disabled`. **Style against this, not
the raw `hovered` intrinsic**, or a disabled control lights up under the pointer. Always
false on touch, since `hovered` is.

## down
The pressed look — the `pressed` intrinsic gated by `disabled`, **with keyboard
activation folded in**, so Space/Enter flashes the same appearance a pointer press
gives. The other half of the styling pair with `hot`.

## focused
True while this control holds keyboard focus. For the *ring*, you want nothing: the
app-level `FocusRing` indicates focus for you. Read this only for a control's own
focus styling.

## focusVisible
Focused **and** the focus arrived by keyboard — the web's `:focus-visible` channel.
Cleared by blur and by a pointer press on this control, so a clicked control shows no
keyboard edge while a tabbed one does. What a `Pane` header's focus edge reads.

## iconLeft
A decorative icon for the leading slot, **named by class** (`iconLeft = "TrashIcon"`),
not nested as a child — a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form where authored
and data-bound are the same mechanism (`iconLeft = { "" + :icon }` in a replicated
toolbar). Control only declares the slot; the concrete control lays it out. A
**computed** name needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build, since no static reference
reaches it.

## iconRight
The trailing icon slot, same vocabulary as `iconLeft`. Setting it **wins over the
chevron a `menu` would imply** — see `rightIcon`.

## menu
The menu this control drops — an instance, not a name (`menu = { app.optionsMenu }`).
Setting it is a *role*, not decoration: the disclosure mark, the anchored open below
the control, the held-open fill, and ArrowDown-to-open all follow together. **Declare
one menu and point many controls at it** rather than one per opener; the menu reads

`Menu`'s items and `DataGrid`'s columns:

### Why data, and not `Segment` children

Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know
which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask
the view tree that: `childViews` carries **set membership only**, so `.length` is
live while anything reaching into the collection is refused —
`aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]`.
The compiler names the answer.

picks from a `ForEach`, Ant Design takes `options`; only Material and WinUI name
the item at all, and both compound it. A bare `Segment` class was the minority
pattern — and bare enough that two apps in this corpus had taken the name for a
paragraph of prose.

Segments divide the control's width evenly. This is a DESIGN decision and it
could be otherwise: a `Layout`'s `place()` may aggregate over children — that is
how `SimpleLayout` sizes a variable-width row — so a strategy that placed each
segment by its own label and interpolated the pill between neighbours is
buildable. The `DECLARE7001` refusal binds constraints reaching into the view

- **The systems that call this a segmented control agree.** UIKit divides evenly

  segmented `Picker`. The ones that size to content — Bootstrap, Ant — are really

  similar in length. Equal width enforces that rather than tolerating it. One long
  label makes the whole control look wrong, which is the feedback you want.

  variable widths it would have to morph its width WHILE travelling, which reads
  as rubbery and worsens the more the labels differ. Most platforms never meet
  this, because their highlight pops.

its labels.** Set `width`, or accept `segMin × choices.length`.

place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. Calendar's tab
strip discovered this; it is the one thing the bespoke copies did better than the
library, and it is now here.

a hairline. The motion is calendar's. Neither app was wrong about the half it got
right (`chrome-divergences.md` D9).

App [ fill = { this.theme.bg }, textColor = { this.theme.text }, minWidth = 320, appName = "Declare Tracker",

    // ── the responsive facts ───────────────────────────────────────────────

    compact: boolean = { this.root.width < 640 },      // the bar: brand compacts, omnibox shrinks

    barH: number = 56,
    footRowH: number = 32,        // the editor footer's one row height
    footLabelPx: number = 16,     // …and its button-label size, the baseline reference
    railW: number = 300,
    railOn: boolean = { this.root.width >= 1100 },     // below this the rail yields to the list

    // ── the chrome facts (the flagship family conventions) ─────────────────

    themeMode: string = "auto",
    darkUI: boolean = { this.themeMode == "dark" || (this.themeMode == "auto" && this.root.dark) },
    theme = { this.root.darkUI ? Themes.sanFrancisco(true) : Themes.sanFrancisco(false) },

    // ── THE TRUTH ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    //
    // `db` holds the issues, and that is the whole of it: a verb writes db and
    // every projection that read db re-runs. Nothing else anywhere holds data.
    //
    // This used to hang off a `rev` counter every verb bumped, threaded through
    // nine method parameters, on the stated grounds that "a method's reads are
    // not tracked — the ARGUMENTS are the wiring". That reason was FALSE: the
    // compiler reads through method bodies (declare.md §5), and a method here
    // wires `this.root.db.read(["issues"])` with no help. What the clock was
    // really covering for is one line — `issuesOf` used to read
    // `db.value.issues`, a raw property walk off the value with no cell to
    // subscribe to, so the projection never woke. `read([…])` is the region
    // read the language tracks. One spelling, and the clock was redundant.

    db: Dataset { { "issues": [] } },

    src: DataSource [ url = "issues.json" ],

    booted: boolean = false,
    loadMs: number = 0,
    adoptMs: number = 0,

    onInit() {
        const t0 = trkNow()
        this.src.fetch().then(() => {
            const t1 = trkNow()
            this.adopt(this.src.value != null ? this.src.value.issues : [])
            this.loadMs = Math.round(t1 - t0)
            this.adoptMs = Math.round(trkNow() - t1)
            this.booted = true
            })
        },

    adopt(issues: array) {
        for (const it of issues) {
            }
        this.db.set(["issues"], issues)
        this.takeSelection(null)
        this.closeDetail()
        },

    regenerate(count: number) {
        const t0 = trkNow()
        const issues = trkGenerate(count)
        const t1 = trkNow()
        this.adopt(issues)
        this.loadMs = Math.round(t1 - t0)
        this.adoptMs = Math.round(trkNow() - t1)
        },

    // ── the view facts ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    sortOn: string = "updated",
    sortDir: string = "desc",
    groupBy: string = "none",                    // none | status
    fStatus: string = "",                        // "" = no filter
    fAssignee: string = "",
    fLabel: string = "",

    // A filter, sort, or grouping change is a NEW arrangement, not an edit
    // to the old one — the list starts it at the top. The runtime pins the
    // viewport to its anchor row across DATA changes (so an edit never
    // yanks the reader); a rearrangement is the one case where that
    // stability is wrong, so the reset is written twice: once now, and
    // once after the new projection has settled under the anchor logic.

    rearranged() {
        this.list.scrollY = 0
        setTimeout(() => { this.list.scrollY = 0 }, 0)
        },

    // Is the keyboard currently owned by a text field? A bare-character
    // shortcut must never steal a keystroke from one. `placeholder` is
    // declared by TextInput alone, so its presence identifies an editor
    // without the App needing to know where every field in the tree is.

    typing() -> boolean {
        const f = Focus.getFocus()
        return f != null && (f).placeholder !== undefined
        },

    clearAll() {
        this.fStatus = ""; this.fAssignee = ""; this.fLabel = ""; this.query = ""
        this.bar.omni.text = ""
        this.rearranged()
        },

    toggleFilter(facet: string, value: string) {
        if (facet == "status") this.fStatus = this.fStatus == value ? "" : value
        else if (facet == "assignee") this.fAssignee = this.fAssignee == value ? "" : value
        else if (facet == "label") this.fLabel = this.fLabel == value ? "" : value
        this.rearranged()
        },

    setSort(field: string) {
        if (this.sortOn != field) { this.sortOn = field; this.sortDir = field == "title" ? "asc" : "desc" }
        this.rearranged()
        },

    toggleSortDir() {
        this.sortDir = this.sortDir == "desc" ? "asc" : "desc"
        this.rearranged()
        },

    // collapsed groups — a plain array behind a change clock. This clock is
    // REAL, unlike the data one that used to sit above: `_collapsed` is an
    // ordinary JS array stashed on the instance, not a reactive slot, so
    // nothing can notice it change and something has to say so. The honest fix
    // is to make it a slot; until then the counter is doing actual work.

    groupRev: number = 0,
    collapsedSet() -> array { return (this)._collapsed ?? ((this)._collapsed = []) },
    isCollapsed(s: string, g: number) -> boolean { return this.collapsedSet().includes(s) },
    toggleGroup(s: string) {
        const c = this.collapsedSet()
        const i = c.indexOf(s)
        if (i < 0) c.push(s); else c.splice(i, 1)
        this.groupRev = this.groupRev + 1
        },

    // ── THE PROJECTION — the one derived dataset the list renders.
    //    filter → sort → (group); group headers are records too ({ kind:
    //    "hdr" }) — non-uniform rows are just rows.
    //
    //    The arguments are the VIEW FACTS, and they are arguments because that
    //    reads well, not because the wiring needs them: the body could read
    //    `app.query` directly and wire identically. The DATA is not among them
    //    — `project` reaches it through `issuesOf`, and the compiler follows
    //    the call. ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    shown: Dataset [ contents = { this.root.project(this.root.fStatus, this.root.fAssignee, this.root.fLabel, this.root.query, this.root.sortOn, this.root.sortDir, this.root.groupBy, this.root.groupRev) } ],

    issuesOf() -> array { return this.db.read(["issues"]) ?? [] },

    project(byStatus: string, byAssignee: string, byLabel: string, query: string, sortOn: string, sortDir: string, grouping: string, groupClock: number) -> object {
        let rows = this.issuesOf()
        if (byStatus != "" || byAssignee != "" || byLabel != "") {
            rows = rows.filter((it) =>
                (byStatus == "" || (it).status == byStatus) &&
                (byAssignee == "" || (it).assignee == byAssignee) &&
                (byLabel == "" || (((it).labels ?? [])).includes(byLabel)))
            }
        // the query NARROWS like any other filter (a tracker searches by
        // hiding what doesn't match, not by bolding what does); the scan is
        // timed and the number rides out with the value — pure, no clocks
        let searchMs = 0
        if (query.trim() != "") {
            const t0 = trkNow()
            const needle = query.trim().toLowerCase()
            const hay = ((this)._hay ??= new WeakMap())
            rows = rows.filter((it) => {
                let h = hay.get(it)
                if (h == null || (h).u != (it).updated) {
                    h = ({ u: (it).updated, s: ((it).title + "\n" + ((it).description ?? "") + "\n" + (((it).labels ?? [])).join(" ") + "\n" + ((it).assignee ?? "")).toLowerCase() })
                    hay.set(it, h)
                    }
                return (h).s.includes(needle)
                })
            searchMs = Math.max(0, Math.round((trkNow() - t0) * 10) / 10)
            }
        // Every comparator is ASCENDING — least-interesting first: oldest,
        // lowest priority, A→Z. `desc` then reverses, uniformly, with no key
        // carrying a special case (so a new sort field inherits the rule).
        const RANK = ({ P0: 3, P1: 2, P2: 1, P3: 0 })
        const asc = sortOn == "priority" ? (a, b) => (RANK)[(a).priority] - (RANK)[(b).priority] || (a).updated - (b).updated
            : sortOn == "title" ? (a, b) => ((a).title < (b).title ? -1 : (a).title > (b).title ? 1 : 0)
            : (a, b) => (a).updated - (b).updated
        rows = [...rows].sort(sortDir == "desc" ? (a, b) => asc(b, a) : asc)
        if (grouping != "status") return ({ rows: rows, total: rows.length, searchMs: searchMs })
        const order = ["open", "in-progress", "blocked", "closed"]
        const collapsed = this.collapsedSet()
        const out = []
        for (const st of order) {
            const members = rows.filter((it) => (it).status == st)
            if (members.length == 0) continue
            out.push(({ kind: "hdr", id: "hdr:" + st, status: st, count: members.length }))
            if (!collapsed.includes(st)) out.push(...members)
            }
        return ({ rows: out, total: rows.length, searchMs: searchMs })
        },

    closedPerDay() -> object {

        const issues = this.issuesOf()
        for (const it of issues) if (((it).updated ?? 0) > maxU) maxU = (it).updated
        const today = Math.floor(maxU / DAY)
        const days = new Array(14).fill(0)
        for (const it of issues) {
            const c = (it).closedAt
            if (c == null) continue
            const d = today - Math.floor(c / DAY)
            if (d >= 0 && d < 14) days[13 - d] = days[13 - d] + 1
            }
        return ({ days: days, peak: Math.max(1, ...days) })
        },

        const c = ({ open: 0, "in-progress": 0, blocked: 0, closed: 0 })
